subject: research/selfrep-recyclers
professional: a distributed-recycling researcher of the Recyclebot / Precious Plastic kind (someone who has built and costed a shredder-extruder line, e.g. in Joshua Pearce's group), together with a mechanical engineer who has specified a small shredder. They would check first whether the shredder, extruder and furnace bills of materials resemble machines that actually run, whether the payback currency (kilograms of imports) is the one that matters, and whether the work cites the Recyclebot literature.

evidence.correctness: Ran python3 experiments/run.py inputs through an independent script (scratchpad ind.py) that re-derived every figure from selfrep_closure's parts list and the Params defaults, not from selfrep_materials.balance. Reproduced: plastic saving 0.0978 kg/copy (1.10 kg printed plastic, F=1.222 kg, saving 0.08F); aluminium saving 0.069 kg/copy (0.175 kg Al stock, offcuts 0.075 kg x 0.92); printer-alone import 9.64 kg and payback 98.6 -> 99 copies; router+laser import 4.97 + 0.667 + 4.0/0.7 = 11.35 kg -> 116 copies; furnace 6.5/0.069 = 94 copies; eol=0.5/1.0 with phi=0.3 and 0.8 gives 31, 21 and 12 copies (11.6 rounds to 12). All match results.txt, so the arithmetic is right. Capped at 2 because every driver (machine masses, which parts are vitamins) is an invented placeholder, and the Monte Carlo (masses only, factor 0.5 to 2) leaves the saving side fixed, so the quoted 91 to 164 interval understates uncertainty. The README sentence 'a printer copy's own 4.9 to 5.3 kg' of vitamins was not rechecked.
evidence.completeness: Checked each README claim: 8 unittest tests run and pass; experiments/run.py writes results.txt with all five sections the README quotes; payback.svg exists; machine part lists for three machines, payback by shop, eol/phi sweep and Monte Carlo are all present and match the README's Results bullets. Not claimed and absent: cost or time payback, fleet retirement, closure integration (all listed under Next steps). README does not link figure payback.svg. Nothing is a stub.
evidence.verification: python3 -m unittest discover -s tests: 8 tests, OK. Three seeded mutations in machines.py, each reverted (git status of the project directory clean afterwards): (1) paybacks() numerator doubled, '2 * imp / pl': all 8 tests passed, NOT caught. (2) machine_import_kg sheet feedstock divided by y_metal changed to 'v += m' (yield ignored): all 8 passed, NOT caught. (3) filament feedstock 1/(1-s) changed to 1/(1+s): caught by test_import_at_least_mass. No test asserts a payback value, an import figure, or anything in results.txt; the only quantitative checks are two loose delta=0.02/0.03 comparisons against the sibling project's text. The Monte Carlo is untested.
evidence.craft: Read machines.py, tests/test_recyclers.py, experiments/run.py. Readable, small, stdlib only, docstrings state the assumptions. Defects: sys.path.insert of sibling src trees at import time in machines.py (and again in selfrep_materials), so the package is not installable despite its pyproject.toml; run.py's Monte Carlo mutates the module-global MACHINES dict and rebuilds Part objects with a positional 9-argument constructor, which breaks silently if Part gains a field; machine_import_kg duplicates the made/vitamin split already in machine_mass_kg; 'paybacks' returns None for zero saving and the caller's fmt handles it but the Monte Carlo sorts a list that could contain None; tests import SHOPS through machines rather than from the source. No dead code of note.
evidence.claims: Backed: the headline numbers (99, 116, 94, 31, 12 copies; 91 to 164) all appear in results.txt and reproduce. Honest: README says 'Stylised, assumed', says mass is the only currency, and lists owner steps. Not backed or weak: 'the plastic recyclers do not pay back in any sensible time' and the closing message that recycling is 'an early-stage distraction' are stated as conclusions although they follow from invented machine masses (a 6.75 kg shredder) and a mass-only currency; the README claims it follows von Neumann and Freitas and Merkle but cites no recycling literature at all. grep for Recyclebot, Precious Plastic and Pearce in research/selfrep-* returns nothing. 'No published shredder, extruder or furnace design is reproduced' is true, which is the problem rather than a virtue.
evidence.fitness: A researcher cannot build on it as it stands. The machine part lists are placeholders, so the output is a function of the invented list; there is no data a follow-up could reuse and no BOM from any open design. Nearest prior work is not named: Baechler, DeVuono and Pearce 2013 (Recyclebot, distributed recycling of waste polymer into RepRap feedstock); Kreiger, Mulder, Glover and Pearce 2014 (life cycle analysis of distributed recycling of post-consumer HDPE); Zhong and Pearce 2018 (distributed recycling and manufacturing co-evolution); Precious Plastic open machine designs, which publish full shredder and extruder BOMs and masses; Jones et al. 2011 (RepRap) is cited. A reader would learn only that 'payback is about 100 copies if the assumed machines weigh what the author guessed'. The one transferable idea, that payback should be measured against the shop's own scrap versus retired plastic (eol), is correct and useful but is a one-line extension of selfrep-materials.
evidence.domain: Compared against Precious Plastic's published shredder (10 mm steel plates, 2 to 7.5 kW motor and gearbox, typically on the order of 100 kg) and Recyclebot-class extruders (diameter sensor, puller and spooler, controlled cooling). The assumed shredder (6.75 kg total, 0.9 kg of cutters, 2 kg motor) and extruder (2.8 kg, no filament-diameter control, no puller or cooling stage, which is what makes recycled filament printable) are an order of magnitude too light or missing the parts that dominate cost. Recycled PLA or PETG also needs drying, which is absent. Aluminium: a crucible furnace is sized to recover 75 g of offcuts per printer copy, which no metalworker would build; casting only makes sense as a batch. Kilograms of imports is not the currency a practitioner would use (cost, hours and energy would), as the README itself concedes. The structure (payback = import cost / saving per unit) is sound and standard.

defects.what: Machine part lists, which drive every headline payback, are invented and far lighter than real open designs (Precious Plastic shredder on the order of 100 kg vs 6.75 kg assumed), so '99 to 116 copies' and the 'distraction' conclusion are not evidence about real recyclers; no recycling literature is cited or compared.
Tests do not pin any payback or import value: doubling the payback numerator and dropping the sheet-yield division both leave all 8 tests green.

Monte Carlo varies only machine masses, not the saving side (s, r, phi, y_metal) or the part list, so the reported 5 to 95% interval is much narrower than the true uncertainty; README partly discloses this.
Extruder omits the filament-diameter sensor, puller and cooling, the parts that make recycled filament usable; furnace is sized for 75 g of offcuts per copy.
Import-time sys.path hacks for sibling projects while pyproject.toml advertises an installable package with no dependencies; Monte Carlo rebuilds Part with a positional constructor.
README gives no link to experiments/payback.svg and the '4.9 to 5.3 kg printer copy' vitamin figure is not generated by results.txt.

verdict: Not at the bar and, as a research result, not one a researcher can build on. The arithmetic is right: seven figures (plastic and aluminium saving per copy, three paybacks, the eol/phi grid) re-derived from the closure parts list without using the author's balance function all match results.txt. But the numbers are a function of three invented machine part lists that are an order of magnitude lighter than published open shredders and omit the extruder parts that matter, the recycling literature (Recyclebot, Precious Plastic) is never cited, and the headline 'recycling is a distraction' rests on a mass-only currency. The test suite is shallow: of three seeded bugs only one was caught, and neither a doubled payback nor a dropped sheet-yield factor failed anything. Finished (it does what its README lists) but junior-level: scores correctness 2, completeness 3, verification 1, craft 2, claims 2, fitness 1, domain 1. Another session had an uncommitted edit in research/workcell-twin during this audit; it is unrelated and was not touched.
